title: Already rewarded
hookLine: have I done something for the common good? then I've been rewarded (Meditations 11.4)

lines: A RECEIPT BOOK IN YOUR HEAD.
EVERY SLIP SAYS: YOU OWE ME.
cards: Somewhere in most of us there's a receipt book. Drove her to the airport: one slip. Covered his shift: another.

Remembered the birthday, listened for an hour on the phone, lent the ladder and got it back with a dent. Nobody asked us to keep it. We keep it anyway, and every slip says the same thing underneath: you owe me.
Marcus wrote a short note in book eleven that closes the book before the first slip is written.

teach.h: DONE FOR THE COMMON GOOD? PAID.
teach.b: First, the note. Have I done something for the common good? Marcus asks.
Then I've been rewarded. Keep this always at hand, he adds, and never stop. Second, why it's already paid.

teach.h: AN EYE DOESN'T CHARGE FOR SEEING.
teach.b: In book nine he put it sharply: wanting a return for a kindness is like an eye demanding a fee for seeing, or feet for walking. Seeing is what an eye is for.
For Marcus, working with and for others is what a person is for, so the doing is the payment. Third, one letter. In book seven he plays on two Greek words that differ by a single letter.

teach.h: A LIMB, NOT JUST A PART.
teach.b: Melos means a limb, like an arm or a hand. Meros means a part, a piece, like one brick in a pile.
Think of yourself as only a part of humankind, he says, and you don't yet love people from the heart; you do good because it's proper, as a duty.
Think of yourself as a limb of the one body, and doing good becomes doing good to yourself. A hand doesn't send the arm an invoice. Fourth, why it's freeing.
If the reward is in the doing, no one can cheat you or ignore you out of it.
The account is settled the moment you act.
Thanks is still welcome. You just aren't waiting for it.

how: People who take this note seriously often do small, unannounced things for shared spaces and neighbors, and treat the doing itself as the point rather than waiting for thanks.

o: praised by others once they see what you've done
repaid later by the people you helped, if you wait
paid in full by the doing itself, with no return owed

p: doesn't charge a fee for seeing
a limb of the one body

s: Marcus says a good act earns its reward later
he says if you've done something for the common good, you've already been rewarded.
in book seven Marcus plays on two Greek words a single letter apart
melos, a limb, and meros, a part: a limb does good as good to itself.

games.q: you helped fix a shared problem. no one thanked you. you're Marcus. what's your thought?
o: I've done something for the common good, so I'm rewarded already.
games.why: have I done something for the common good? he writes. then I've had my reward. keep this at hand and never stop.

practice: Bring to mind one slip from your own receipt book, a favor you're still quietly waiting to have repaid.
Picture yourself not as a separate piece but as one hand on a body that includes that person too, and let the slip go, just for now.

wordCard.voice: Already rewarded. Marcus's note: have I done something for the common good? Then I've been rewarded already. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a limb. In 7.13 Marcus tells himself to be a limb of humankind, not a mere part (μέρος).

carryVoice: Your line: no invoice. The good you did was paid for the moment you did it. That's day six hundred twenty-two.
